findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reuse the c605 `slow_ls_tree` pattern: save `real_bound` in the `slow_git` fixture closure and let the setter apply `_BOUND_S` only when it arms a hang, instead of storing the bound as an attribute on the setter.
evidence: Plan: "restore the module's production bound (`monkeypatch.setattr(git_fetch, "_GIT_TIMEOUT", <value saved before the fixture shrank it>)`)" and "The fixture records the original value as an attribute of the setter it returns".

tests/unit/test_snapshot_submodules_watchdog_c605.py:81 `real_bound = git_fetch._GIT_TIMEOUT`; lines 85-91: `_set(on)` calls `monkeypatch.setattr(git_fetch, "_GIT_TIMEOUT", _BOUND_S)` only when `on`, otherwise `monkeypatch.setattr(git_fetch, "_GIT_TIMEOUT", real_bound)`; comment at lines 83-84 names civil-fameless-starfish.
The plan itself calls this the "Same class as closed civil-fameless-starfish". That ticket's fix (change 3370, 2102dcfb220) moved the bound into the fixture setter; it did not add per-test overrides.
No test file in the repo stores the original bound as an attribute on a fixture-returned function. The `_GIT_TIMEOUT` search shows only `monkeypatch.setattr` overrides and the c605 closure.
findings.finding: The plan builds a new way to reach the production bound: it stores the original `_GIT_TIMEOUT` as an attribute on the setter function, and the test reads it back and calls `monkeypatch.setattr` itself. The repo already has a working fix for this exact bug class in `test_snapshot_submodules_watchdog_c605.py`. There, a closure variable holds the real bound, and the setter applies the 1 s bound only while a hang is on and restores the real bound otherwise. The function-attribute pattern is used nowhere else and has one user, so it is premature (Rule of Three). It also means each future healthy-path test must remember to undo the bound by hand, instead of the fixture doing it.
findings.location: Approach — "The fixture records the original value as an attribute of the setter it returns, so the test does not hard-code it."; tests/unit/test_snapshot_git_watchdog_d33f.py `slow_git` fixture (lines 40-65)
scenarios: A later healthy-path test in d33f uses `slow_git` and forgets to read the setter attribute and reset the bound. It again holds real git to 1 s and flakes on loaded runners.
Someone maintaining both watchdog test files finds two different fixes for the same bug and cannot tell which one to copy.

Add a comment citing this ticket and civil-fameless-starfish, as c605 does.

findings.finding: The plan misses a better approach that the codebase already uses. The sibling fix for the same bug class shrinks _GIT_TIMEOUT only when a slow subcommand is switched on. The plan instead keeps the fixture's unconditional shrink and has one test set the bound back, using a value stored as an attribute on the setter. That fixes only this one test and leaves the trap in place for any future test that uses slow_git for working git calls.
scenarios: A future test in this module uses slow_git for working git calls, or makes a healthy call after arming, and hits the same 1 s timeout on a loaded Windows or CI runner.

Someone reading the healthy test sees the fixture shrink the bound and the test set it back, with the original value kept on a function attribute. That is harder to follow than the sibling file's on/off setter.

Have test_healthy_calls_still_answer call slow_git(None), or arm nothing, so the wrapper still passes calls through while the production bound applies. Leave the slowed tests unchanged.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Keep a discriminating check in the healthy test: assert the armed slowdown was never triggered for the healthy calls, and add an AC showing the test still fails when the slowdown is deliberately armed on a healthy subcommand.
evidence: "restore the module's production bound ... so the healthy calls are judged against the bound production uses"
"after arming the fixture with an unrelated subcommand"
No AC or step asserts that the armed slowdown did NOT apply to the healthy calls.
findings.finding: Restoring the production bound in test_healthy_calls_still_answer may remove the test's ability to detect its target regression. The test asserts that arming the watchdog for one subcommand does not affect unrelated ones. Under the 1 s bound, a fixture that wrongly slows the healthy calls makes them time out, so the test fails. Under the much larger production bound, the same leak (the fixture's injected delay is presumably sized to exceed 1 s, not the production bound) just makes the calls slower, and the test passes. The plan adds no replacement assertion.
scenarios: A future fixture or watchdog change makes the slowdown match every git subcommand. The healthy test still passes, just several seconds slower, so the regression ships undetected.
findings.suggested_fix: After restoring the production bound, add an assertion that the slowed subcommand's delay was not hit during the healthy calls. Options: a marker or counter the fixture's slow path records, or each healthy call's elapsed time staying below the fixture's injected sleep. Add an AC: temporarily arming the fixture with `remote`, or with a matching-all pattern, makes the healthy test fail.

evidence: "a PATH git shim that sleeps 1.2 s before every start makes the healthy test fail with `timed out after 1s` before the change and pass after"
Approach: "arming the fixture with an unrelated subcommand" — the fixture has its own slowing mechanism, and its interaction with an external PATH shim is not stated.
findings.finding: The reproduction fixture's validity is under-specified. The plan does not say how the 1.2 s PATH git shim is installed alongside the slow_git fixture's own subcommand-slowing mechanism, or on which platform it runs. As a result, nothing guarantees the shim's delay actually applies to the four healthy git calls, both before and after the change.
scenarios: The fixture puts its own git wrapper ahead of PATH, or resolves the real git by absolute path, so the 1.2 s shim never runs. The 'before' run then does not fail for the stated reason, or the 'after' pass proves nothing.
The shim is a POSIX script, but the flake is Windows-specific. Windows subprocess resolution needs a .cmd/.exe shim, so the reproduction does not run as described.

Evidence class: Unverified. The shim's platform and PATH placement are not specified, and I could not run it.
findings.finding: The reproduction depends on a new test-harness capability: a git shim on PATH that sleeps 1.2 s before every start. The plan does not say which platform it runs on or where the shim goes on PATH. On Windows, where the failure happened, a shell-script shim named 'git' is not found by subprocess/CreateProcess. And because slow_git runs shutil.which('git') when it sets up and puts its own wrapper first on PATH, the delay applies only if the shim is already ahead of the real git before the fixture runs. If either condition is missed, the healthy test passes 'before' as well, and the before/after acceptance criterion cannot be shown.
findings.location: Testing / Acceptance Criteria line 1 ('Under the 1.2 s-per-start shim the healthy test fails before and passes after')
scenarios: The author runs the reproduction on a Windows runner with a sh shim. CreateProcess ignores the shim, all git calls run at normal speed, and the 'before' run passes, so the AC cannot be met.
The shim is put on PATH after pytest starts, or after the real git on PATH. real_git resolves to the real binary, there is no delay, and the 'before' run passes.
findings.suggested_fix: In Testing, add: 'Run on Linux: create $SHIM/git as `#!/bin/sh\nsleep 1.2\nexec /usr/bin/git "$@"`, then run `PATH=$SHIM:$PATH pytest tests/unit/test_snapshot_git_watchdog_d33f.py::test_healthy_calls_still_answer`. The slow_git fixture's real_git resolves to the shim, so every healthy call pays the delay.'
